summary: This informational document registers a formal Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for assignment by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), as specified in RFC 3406. It is used mainly to identify XML-related objects.

eli5.summary: NATO needed its own naming system so that its digital documents and items get unique names that nobody else uses. This registers it.

questions: what is the urn nato namespace
subtitle: NATO registers the formal URN namespace identifier "nato" so its XML message specifications get stable, unique names.

tldr.problem: NATO publishes many XML message definitions and service specifications, and without its own namespace identifier they risk using local, self-made URN namespaces that can collide.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the formal URN namespace ID "nato" with a syntax of Type, optional Source and further segments, handed out by the NATO Naming and Registration Authority.
tldr.outcome: NATO XML artefacts can be named with persistent, managed names of the form urn:nato:... The document is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 7467 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the RFC metadata. It records the registration of the nato URN namespace.

sections.title: Why NATO Needs a Namespace
sections.content:
NATO has long used standardised, character-oriented message text formats (MTF) to exchange information among its commands and with national entities, commercial partners and non-governmental organisations. Almost 400 NATO-defined messages are listed in the APP-11 NATO Message Catalogue.

Since 2008 the catalogue has also included XML definitions of these messages, which created a need to define and manage a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for naming the XML namespaces. This document requests a formal URN namespace as described in Section 4.3 of RFC 3406.
sections.eli5: NATO sends many kinds of standard messages. Now that they are written in XML, each needs a proper, lasting name.

sections.title: The urn:nato Syntax
sections.content:
IANA has assigned the Namespace ID (NID) nato. After urn:nato:, the namespace specific string is a Type, optionally followed by a Source, optionally followed by any number of further segments, all separated by colons.

The Type is required and names a category of resource, such as mtf. The Source belongs to a Type and names a particular standard, catalogue or other specification; not every Type has Sources yet. Each segment is made of letters, digits, a set of allowed punctuation characters, or percent-encoded bytes, but never a colon, and must conform to the URN syntax of RFC 2141.
sections.eli5: A NATO name is built like a street address: the big category first, then the smaller part, then more detail, with colons between the pieces.

sections.title: Registration, Uniqueness and Persistence
sections.content:
The NATO Naming and Registration Authority (NRA) is the registrar for the first two levels, Type and Source. It may assign segments below those or delegate that work, but it ensures a registry of the resulting namespace is maintained. A name is only assigned when a relevant specification advances, and the registrar checks requests against existing registrations.

The NRA directly ensures global uniqueness. A URN is assigned to at most one resource and is never reassigned; the registry records whether it is "active" or "archive". Lexical equivalence follows RFC 2141, and the scope is global.

The namespace is not currently listed with a Resolution Discovery System. The RFC says that in future, URNs may be resolved through a NATO listing, a third-party resolver, a private resolver, or a mix.
sections.eli5: One office hands out the names and keeps a list. A name is given to only one thing and never reused, so there are no mix-ups.

sections.title: Community and Namespace Considerations
sections.content:
Without a registered NID, NATO specifications might be placed in locally relevant, self-generated URN namespaces. The RFC says this hurts portability and adoption and risks name collisions when messages reach the global federation of partners. A dedicated namespace also lets NATO use URNs for persistent naming of non-XML resources.

The standards are NATO-published but come from consensus of multi-national working groups, are implemented in commercial products, and are used by partners internationally. The Message Text Formats Capability Team that maintains the MTF standards is described as open in principle to recognised NATO Partners around the globe.
sections.eli5: If every group invented its own naming, two groups might pick the same name by accident. One shared naming system avoids that.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The URNs are opaque, so there are no extra security considerations beyond those of URIs and URNs in general (STD 66, RFC 2141, BCP 66). The RFC notes that resolving a NATO URN through a resolver not operated or delegated by NATO may return outdated, incorrect or confusing results. The specification is for public use and not subject to NATO security policies.

For IANA, the formal NID nato is entered in the Formal URN Namespaces registry. Formal NIDs are assigned via IETF Consensus and IESG review. The registration is Version 1, dated 2014-09-11.
sections.eli5: The names are just labels, so they bring no new danger. Just ask NATO's own lookup service, since others might give a wrong answer.
